title: MARL2Grid-TR: A Multi-Agent RL Benchmark in Power Grid Operations
claim: A localized discrete action on one agent's component can relieve an overloaded element in a system controlled by multiple decentralized agents.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, big arrow between, red highlights for overload and action
description: Two side-by-side copies of the same toy four-node power grid, linked by a thick black arrow pointing left to right. Nodes S1 to S4 are circles joined by lines labeled with power flows in MW. Dashed boxes group the nodes into Agent 1 (top) and Agent 2 (bottom). Colored icons show a green power plant and a factory as generators (400 MW and 100 MW) on the left. A shop and a robot-car assembly line are loads (-200 MW and -300 MW) on the right. In the left panel, the S1-S2 line is red at 236 MW, labeled 'line overload!'. In the right panel, a bus split at S2 (a black dot inside a dashed red ellipse) brings the flow to 200 MW. All lines turn green, and Agent 2 is labeled 'idle'. The eye goes first to the red line, then to the arrow, then to the red ellipse.
caption: Toy example of a grid controlled by two agents, where all transmission lines have maximum capacities of 210 MW. A “bus split” topological (discrete) action addresses an overloaded line (red).
abstract: Improving power grid operations is essential for enhancing flexibility and accelerating grid decarbonization. Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise in this domain, most notably through the Learning to Run a Power Network (L2RPN) competition series, but prior work has primarily focused on single-agent settings, neglecting the often decentralized, multi-agent nature of grid control. We fill this gap with MARL2Grid-TR, the first multi-agent RL (MARL) benchmark for grid topology and redispatching, developed in collaboration with transmission system operators. Built on RTE France’s high-fidelity simulation platform, our benchmark supports decentralized control across substations and generators, with configurable agent scopes, observability settings, expert-informed heuristics, and safety-critical constraints. The benchmark includes a suite of realistic scenarios that expose key challenges, such as coordination under partial information, long-horizon objectives, and adherence to hard physical constraints. Empirical results show that current MARL methods struggle under these real-world conditions. By providing a standardized, extensible platform, we aim to advance the development of scalable, cooperative, and safe learning algorithms for power grids.
